title: Is this genome good enough?
text: Goal: for each sample, gather the quality numbers in one table, then take a decision: is the genome usable for phylogenetics (Day 4), does it need review or re-sequencing, or must it be discarded? A genome is never “good” or “bad” in itself: it is good enough for a purpose, judged on a handful of numbers.

title: Is this genome good enough?
text:
The numbers that matter







Metric
Why it matters




Total reads / % mapped
how much data, and how much of it is the virus (low % = contamination, poor enrichment)


Mean depth
average confidence of the base calls


% of genome ≥ 10x (breadth)
how much of the genome can really be called


% N and longest run of N
missing information; a long run = a whole region (gene) is missing


Negative control
are there viral reads where there should be none?

title: Is this genome good enough?
text:
Step 1 — Build the summary table
This one command collects, for every sample, the numbers you computed in the previous exercises:
printf "sample\ttotal_reads\tpct_mapped\tmean_depth\tpct_ge10x\tN_bases\tlongest_N_run\n" > results/qc_summary.tsv
for s in S01 S02 S03 S04 S05; do
  total=$(samtools view -c -F 2304 results/bam/$s.bam)
  mapped=$(samtools view -c -F 2308 results/bam/$s.bam)
  pm=$(awk -v m=$mapped -v t=$total 'BEGIN{printf "%.1f", 100*m/t}')
  dp=$(awk '{t+=$3; if($3>=10) n++} END{printf "%.1f\t%.1f", t/NR, 100*n/NR}' results/coverage/$s.depth.tsv)
  nb=$(grep -v '>' results/consensus/$s.fa | tr -cd 'N' | wc -c)
  run=$(grep -v '>' results/consensus/$s.fa | tr -d '\n' | grep -o 'N\+' | awk '{print length}' | sort -n | tail -1)
  printf "%s\t%s\t%s\t%s\t%s\t%s\n" "$s" "$total" "$pm" "$dp" "$nb" "${run:-0}" >> results/qc_summary.tsv
done
column -t -s $'\t' results/qc_summary.tsv
(samtools view -c -F 2304 counts the primary reads; -F 2308 the primary reads that are mapped.)
Cross-check: compare your table with precomputed/qc_summary.tsv (same numbers, plus a PASS / REVIEW / FAIL column).

title: Is this genome good enough?
text:
Step 3 — Discussion questions
1. Which sample would you re-sequence, and what would you change?






TipAnswer






S03: re-sequence from a new library with more input material (re-extract, concentrate the RNA, more reads in the pool) — it has only 5x depth, repeating the same run will not help.
S02: do not repeat everything: re-amplify only the failed region (around 3,500–5,000). Check whether a known mutation falls in a primer site; if so, add or redesign primers, or use a different primer scheme for this lineage.
S04: the genome is complete; the question is the laboratory source of the off-target reads (host DNA, contaminated reagents). Consider host depletion or a cleaner extraction, and identify the reads with Kraken2.




2. What do you report about the negative control?






TipAnswer





Always report it, even if it looks “clean”. Say: the number of reads in the NTC (450), how many map to the virus (50, i.e. 25 pairs), their likely origin (barcode bleed from S01, whose variants they carry), and the consequence for the run: samples with a signal close to that level (S03) cannot be interpreted; high-depth samples (S01, S02, S04) are not affected. If the contamination were larger than a few reads, the whole run should be repeated.



3. Which thresholds would you set for your own laboratory?






TipAnswer





There is no universal answer; the thresholds depend on what the genome is used for:

Lineage assignment: tolerates more N (as long as the lineage-defining positions are covered), e.g. ≥ 80–90 % of the genome.
Phylogenetics and transmission: stricter, e.g. ≥ 90–95 % of the genome at ≥ 10–20x, no long run of N.
Negative controls: a maximum number of viral reads (e.g. ≤ 10), or a ratio to the samples.

Write them down, test them on known samples (positive controls, replicates), apply them the same way to every run, and review them when the protocol changes.

title: Mapping
text:
Goal: Align trimmed SARS-CoV-2 reads to the reference genome, evaluate mapping statistics, and inspect aligned reads in a genome browser.
Activate the course environment:
In this exercise, we use the paired-end reads from NCBI run SRR26396743, cleaned in the previous session, and the SARS-CoV-2 reference genome NC_045512.2.

title: Mapping
text:
Step 1 — Index the reference genome
BWA requires an index to align reads efficiently. Samtools also creates a FASTA index, which is useful for downstream analysis and visualization.
bwa index data/SARS-CoV-2_NC_045512.2.fasta
samtools faidx data/SARS-CoV-2_NC_045512.2.fasta
Questions

What files are created by bwa index?
What is the purpose of the .fai file?
Why do we index the reference before mapping?







TipAnswers






bwa index creates auxiliary index files that allow BWA to search the reference efficiently.
samtools faidx creates a FASTA index (.fai) containing sequence names, lengths, and file offsets.
Indexing avoids rebuilding the reference search structures every time we map reads.

title: Mapping
text:
Step 2 — Map the trimmed reads
Create an output directory:
mkdir -p results/bam
Run BWA-MEM and sort the resulting alignments with Samtools:
bwa mem -t 2 \
  -R '@RG\tID:SRR26396743\tSM:SARS-CoV-2' \
  data/NC_045512.2.fasta \
  results/trimmed/SRR26396743_1.fastq.gz \
  results/trimmed/SRR26396743_2.fastq.gz \
  | samtools sort -@ 2 \
      -o results/bam/SRR26396743.bam -
Index the sorted BAM file:
samtools index results/bam/SRR26396743.bam
Calculate the mapping statistics and save them:
samtools flagstat results/bam/SRR26396743.bam \
  | tee results/bam/SRR26396743.flagstat.txt
What do these commands do?

bwa mem aligns the paired-end reads to the reference genome.
-t 2 uses two threads for BWA.
-R adds read-group information, including the run and sample identifiers.
samtools sort sorts alignments by genomic coordinate and writes a BAM file.
samtools index creates an index for the BAM file.
samtools flagstat summarizes alignment and pairing statistics.
tee displays the results and saves them to a text file.

Questions

What is the difference between a FASTQ file and a BAM file?
Why do we use a reference genome?
Why are the reads sorted after alignment?

Answers
FASTQ files contain read sequences and their base-quality scores. BAM files contain alignment records, including read positions, mapping information, and flags.
The reference genome provides the coordinate system used to locate reads along the viral genome.
Sorting arranges the alignments by genomic position, making downstream analysis and regional access more efficient.

title: Mapping
text:
Step 3 — Read the mapping statistics
Display the report:
cat results/bam/SRR26396743.flagstat.txt
Pay particular attention to these lines:

in total: total number of alignment records examined.
mapped: number and percentage of mapped alignment records.
properly paired: number and percentage of records belonging to pairs aligned in the expected orientation and distance.
primary: primary alignment records, excluding secondary and supplementary alignments.

Remember that samtools flagstat reports alignment records, not necessarily read pairs. For paired-end data, one read pair normally produces two alignment records.
You can also obtain a compact summary of the BAM file:
samtools idxstats results/bam/SRR26396743.bam
The output lists reference sequences, their lengths, the number of mapped records, and the number of unmapped records associated with each reference.
Questions

What percentage of alignment records are mapped?
What percentage are properly paired?
How many alignment records are unmapped?
Does the mapping result suggest that the reads are compatible with the SARS-CoV-2 reference?
What other factors could explain a low mapping percentage?

Answers
Use the values obtained from your own run. Do not assume a particular mapping percentage before analyzing the data.
A high mapping percentage indicates that many reads align to the reference, but it does not by itself prove that the sample is free of contamination or that the resulting genome is accurate.
A low mapping percentage may reflect low-quality reads, residual adapters, a reference mismatch, contamination, or a dataset that does not contain the expected organism.

title: Mapping
section: Step 4 — Visualize the alignments in IGV
text:
Step 4 — Visualize the alignments in IGV
IGV (Integrative Genomics Viewer) allows you to inspect aligned reads and compare their bases with the reference genome.
First, confirm that both the BAM file and its index exist:
ls -lh results/bam/SRR26396743.bam*
Open IGV and load the reference genome:

Select Genomes → Load Genome from File…
Choose data/ncbi/SARS-CoV-2_NC_045512.2.fasta.
Select File → Load from File…
Load results/bam/SRR26396743.bam.
Navigate to a genomic region by entering a coordinate, for example NC_045512.2:1000-2000, if that is the chromosome label displayed by IGV.

Zoom in to examine individual reads and their mismatches relative to the reference.
Questions

Do the reads cover the whole reference genome or only some regions?
Can you see bases that differ from the reference?
Are the differences supported by multiple reads?
Do the supporting reads have good base quality?
Can you conclude that a mismatch is a true variant simply because it appears in one read?

Answers
A mismatch may represent a genuine variant, a sequencing error, an alignment artifact, or another technical issue.
Before interpreting a mismatch, examine its supporting read depth, base quality, mapping quality, strand distribution, and position within the reads. A single observation is not sufficient to establish a true variant.
No specific variant positions or allele frequencies are assumed in this exercise; these must be determined from the actual data.

title: Mapping
Mapping
text:
Final question
Why do we sort and index a BAM file?
Answer
Sorting arranges the alignments by genomic coordinate. Indexing creates a lookup structure that allows programs such as IGV and Samtools to access a specific genomic region without scanning the entire file.
Many downstream tools require a coordinate-sorted BAM file and its index.

title: Setup
text:
1. Install Conda (Miniconda)
Conda is a program that installs bioinformatics tools and keeps them in separate environments, so that one project does not break another. We use Miniconda, a lightweight, free Conda installer. We will add the conda-forge and bioconda channels to install the bioinformatics tools required for this course.

Linux
Download and install the latest Miniconda installer for your system:
mkdir -p ~/miniconda-installer
cd ~/miniconda-installer

curl -LO https://repo.anaconda.com/miniconda/Miniconda3-latest-Linux-$(uname -m).sh
bash Miniconda3-latest-Linux-$(uname -m).sh
Follow the instructions. Accept the licence and answer yes when asked whether to initialize Conda. Then close and reopen the terminal.


Mac (Intel or Apple chip)
Download and install Miniconda:
mkdir -p ~/miniconda-installer
cd ~/miniconda-installer

curl -LO https://repo.anaconda.com/miniconda/Miniconda3-latest-MacOSX-$(uname -m).sh
bash Miniconda3-latest-MacOSX-$(uname -m).sh
Follow the instructions. Accept the licence and initialize Conda when prompted. Then close and reopen the terminal.


Configure Conda channels
Run these commands once:
conda config --add channels defaults
conda config --add channels bioconda
conda config --add channels conda-forge
conda config --set channel_priority strict


Check the installation
conda --version
conda info
You should see the Conda version and installation details. The terminal prompt may start with (base).
Note: Miniconda does not include mamba by default. You can use conda instead, or install mamba in the base environment:
conda install -n base -c conda-forge mamba

5. Real data from NCBI (SARS-CoV-2, Rift Valley fever…)
The practice data of this course are small, so that every step runs in seconds. The commands you learn work exactly the same on real public data. Here is how to get some from NCBI.

a) Find a sequencing run

Open the SRA database: https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/sra
Search your pathogene, for example:

Rift Valley fever: "Rift Valley fever virus"[Organism] AND "ILLUMINA"[Platform] AND "PAIRED"[Layout]

Pick a result that is Illumina, paired-end, with a small size (a few hundred MB at most). Note its Run accession: it starts with SRR, ERR or DRR (below we write SRRXXXXXXX: replace it with yours). Read the description to know which protocol was used (amplicon, capture, metagenomics).

title: Build a phylogenetic tree
text:
Step 1 — Build the maximum-likelihood tree
iqtree2 -s results/phylo/aln.fasta -m MFP -B 1000 -T 2 --seed 1 -o TOYV1_ref --prefix results/phylo/tree -redo
What the options mean: -s alignment, -m MFP choose the best model automatically, -B 1000 1,000 ultrafast bootstrap replicates, -T 2 two threads, --seed 1 reproducible result, -o TOYV1_ref root on the reference, --prefix name of the output files.
IQ-TREE writes several files; the useful ones are:
ls results/phylo/tree.*







File
Content




tree.treefile
the tree (Newick format, with bootstrap support)


tree.iqtree
the full report (model chosen, log-likelihood, tree in text)


tree.log
what happened during the run



Which model was chosen?
grep "Best-fit model" results/phylo/tree.iqtree






TipAbout the model





With so few variable sites a simple model (such as HKY or GTR variants) is chosen; the exact choice has almost no impact here. IQ-TREE may also warn that several sequences are identical: this is normal, they end up on the same branch tip.



Plan B (no IQ-TREE): a neighbour-joining tree from SNP distances, good enough to read the course examples (but without bootstrap support):
python3 scripts/12b_tree_fallback.py

Step 2 — Draw the tree

Questions: do the lineages form clean groups on the tree? Where is S01?






TipAnswer





Yes: each lineage forms its own group (clade). TV.3 and the TV.1 background genomes are close to the root; TV.2 and its two descendants TV.2.1 and TV.2.2 form one large clade. S01 is inside the TV.2 group, next to OB10, OB25, OB15 and OB22 (all early genomes of the outbreak).

title: Build a phylogenetic tree
section: Step 3 — Remove the low-quality genome and rebuild
text:
Step 3 — Remove the low-quality genome and rebuild
OB24 has 23 % N. Remove it from the alignment and rebuild the tree:
seqkit grep -v -p OB24 results/phylo/aln.fasta > results/phylo/aln_clean.fasta
iqtree2 -s results/phylo/aln_clean.fasta -m MFP -B 1000 -T 2 --seed 1 -o TOYV1_ref --prefix results/phylo/tree_clean -redo
Question: does the tree change?






TipAnswer





The main groups and their relationships do not change: OB24 was inside the TV.2.2 group, which stays the same without it. But its position had a lower reliability (a lot of missing data means that it can look closer to some genomes than it really is). Excluding it removes a source of doubt and shows that the conclusions do not depend on a poor genome. The excluded genome and the reason must be written in the report.









Warning



With few variable sites there is little resolution: many branches are short and some are supported weakly. A tree is only as good as the alignment and the data behind it.

Final question
Can two genomes of the same lineage still be unrelated cases? Why?

title: Multiple sequence alignment
text:
A multiple sequence alignment puts homologous positions in the same column, so that each column can be compared between genomes. Phylogenetics and SNP counting both start from it.

Consensus genomes obtained by mapping are already on the reference coordinates, but real data also contain indels and different lengths.
MAFFT is a fast, standard aligner for viral genomes.
Always look at the alignment (AliView, Jalview): never trust it blindly.
Columns full of N or gaps carry no information.

Step 1 — Put all the genomes in one file
The dataset has the reference, the 27 outbreak genomes (OB01–OB27) and your S01. The sed command renames the reference header.
mkdir -p results/phylo
sed 's/^>.*/>TOYV1_ref/' data/reference/TOYV1.fasta > results/phylo/all.fasta
cat data/outbreak/sequences.fasta >> results/phylo/all.fasta
cat results/consensus/S01.fa >> results/phylo/all.fasta
grep -c '>' results/phylo/all.fasta
Question: how many sequences are there?






TipAnswer





29 sequences: 1 reference + 27 outbreak genomes + S01.

title: Multiple sequence alignment
text:
Step 2 — Align with MAFFT
mafft --auto --preservecase --thread 2 results/phylo/all.fasta > results/phylo/aln.fasta
(--preservecase keeps our upper-case letters. Plan B without MAFFT: the toy genomes have no insertion or deletion, so python3 scripts/11b_align_fallback.py just checks that all lengths are equal and writes the same file.)
Check the number of sequences and columns:
seqkit stats results/phylo/aln.fasta
Question: how many sequences and how many alignment columns?






TipAnswer





29 sequences × 10,000 columns (no insertion/deletion, so the length of the reference).

title: Multiple sequence alignment
text:
Step 3 — Inspect the alignment
Open results/phylo/aln.fasta in AliView or Jalview (https://www.jalview.org), or print the content of one column with:
seqkit subseq -r 553:553 results/phylo/aln.fasta | seqkit fx2tab | cut -f1,2 | head -10
Questions

S01 differs from the reference at which positions?
Which outbreak genome has a long block of N? Would you keep it?

To answer the second question, compute the percentage of N in each genome:
awk '/^>/{if(name) printf "%s\t%.1f%%\n", name, 100*n/len; name=substr($0,2); n=0; len=0; next} {n+=gsub(/N/,"N"); len+=length($0)} END{printf "%s\t%.1f%%\n", name, 100*n/len}' results/phylo/aln.fasta | sort -k2 -n -r | head -5






TipAnswers






10 positions: the 8 lineage-defining SNPs (553, 3299, 5753, 6605, 6663, 7748, 9419, 9784) plus 2 private SNPs (269 and 7782).
OB24: about 23 % N (a block of ~2,300 N around positions 4,100–6,400, plus scattered N). Its tree position is unreliable. It should be excluded (the course threshold is 10 % N) — and the reason written in the report.

TipAnswer





OB10 and OB25 are closest to S01 (2 SNPs); OB15 and OB22 are at 3 SNPs; OB01 (lineage TV.2.1) is at 7 SNPs. All the closest ones are early TV.2 genomes from Region A. The distance is tiny (2 SNPs) but remember that two genomes at 2 SNPs are not necessarily direct contacts.

Step 3 — See the effect of a bad reference

title: Reference selection
text:
Final question
Why should all the samples of an outbreak be mapped to the same reference?






TipAnswer





Because the differences are measured against the reference, with its coordinates. If each sample used another reference, positions would not correspond, mutations would not be comparable, and differences between references would be mistaken for differences between samples. One common reference = one common coordinate system = genomes you can align and compare.

title: Read a phylogenetic tree
text:
Tips = the genomes you sequenced. Internal nodes = inferred common ancestors.
Branch length = amount of change (substitutions per site), not time (unless the tree is time-scaled).
Clade = an ancestor and all its descendants. Rotating the branches around a node does not change the tree.
Root = where the tree starts. Without a root you cannot say who is ancestral.
Support (bootstrap) = how robust a branch is. With ultrafast bootstrap, a value ≥ 95 is considered strong; be careful with lower values.

title: Read a phylogenetic tree
text:
Exercise — read the tree
The figure below was made from the course data with the plan-B method (neighbour-joining). Open yours too: it should look similar.



Tree coloured by region





Same tree coloured by lineage


Dates and regions are in data/outbreak/metadata.tsv. To sort the genomes by date:
sort -t$'\t' -k2,2 data/outbreak/metadata.tsv | column -t -s $'\t'
Questions

Where is S01? Who are its closest relatives?
How many clusters do you see, and in which regions?
Which part of the tree is the oldest? (use the dates)
Do the Region C cases form one cluster or several? What does it suggest?







TipAnswers






S01 is in the TV.2 group, next to OB10, OB25, OB15 and OB22 (2–3 SNPs away). OB10, OB25 and OB15 are Region A genomes from 2–4 March: S01 (2 March, Region A) fits perfectly with the start of the Region A outbreak. OB22 is a Region C genome (12 March).
Four groups hang from the root: (i) background TV.1 genomes (Regions B and D, January–February), (ii) TV.3 (Region B, February–March), (iii) the TV.2 early group (Region A, with one Region C genome), and, derived from it, (iv) two sub-clades: TV.2.1 (almost all Region A) and TV.2.2 (Region C).
The oldest genomes are the TV.1 ones (January–February) and the TV.3 ones (February–March), close to the root. The TV.2 group starts in early March; TV.2.1 and TV.2.2 appear from late March: the tree order matches the dates.
One main cluster (TV.2.2: 7 genomes, from 25 March) plus two other Region C genomes that belong to other groups (OB22, an early TV.2, and OB14, a TV.2.1). This suggests several links between regions A and C: an introduction of the early TV.2 virus followed by local transmission (the TV.2.2 cluster), and a later exchange (OB14). Direction cannot be proved by the tree alone.

title: Read a phylogenetic tree
text:
Final question
Two genomes are identical. List three explanations other than “A infected B”.






TipAnswer






Too few mutations to tell them apart: viruses change slowly, so unrelated cases can have the same sequence over a short period.
A common source (same event, same contaminated food/animal) that infected both without contact between them.
A common ancestor several steps earlier, with unsampled intermediate cases (you only see part of the chain).
Laboratory contamination or barcode bleed between the two samples.
Missing data: identical on the positions that could be compared (N regions hide differences).

title: Communicating genomic evidence
text: A genome analysis is useful only if the person who has to decide (a ministry, a hospital, a field team) understands it and knows how far to trust it. This module is about turning results into clear and honest statements.

title: Communicating genomic evidence
text:
Principles

Start with the question the decision maker asks, and answer it first.
Combine genomic and epidemiological evidence (dates, places, contacts). Genomes alone rarely prove transmission.
Say how sure you are, and why.
Show the limits: sampling bias, low resolution, missing data, excluded genomes.
Make it reproducible: tool versions, parameters, files.

title: Communicating genomic evidence
text:
Language of certainty







Evidence
Wording




Identical or nearly identical genomes, compatible dates and places
“genomic data are consistent with a common source”


Same lineage, no finer resolution
“we cannot distinguish between local transmission and repeated introductions”


Different lineages
“not consistent with a single chain of transmission”


Low coverage / many N
“insufficient data to conclude”



Avoid: “proves”, “confirms”, “patient X infected patient Y”.

title: Communicating genomic evidence
Communicating genomic evidence
text:
Exercise 1 — Rewrite these statements (20 min)
Rewrite each sentence so that the data support it.

“The Region C genomes prove the outbreak came from Region A.”
“S03 is negative for the virus.”
“The tree shows that S01 infected OB10.”







TipSuggested answers






“The Region C genomes belong to lineages that descend from the lineage first seen in Region A, which is consistent with an introduction from Region A followed by local transmission. Genomic data alone cannot establish the direction; travel and contact data are needed.” (Why: a tree shows relatedness, not direction; “prove” is too strong.)
“S03 gave insufficient data (mean depth 5x, 95 % of the genome undetermined, in a run whose negative control had viral reads). The result is inconclusive, not negative: the sample should be re-sequenced.” (Why: a failed sequencing is not a negative test.)
“S01 and OB10 are closely related (2 SNPs apart) and both belong to the early Region A cluster. This is compatible with a close epidemiological link, but the genomes alone do not show who infected whom.” (Why: no direction; other chains can produce the same pattern.)

title: Communicating genomic evidence
section: Exercise 2 — Write a key message (15 min)
text:
Exercise 2 — Write a key message (15 min)
Write two sentences that answer: “Where does S01 fit in the outbreak, and how sure are you?”






TipExample





“S01 (Region A, 2 March) belongs to lineage TV.2, the early lineage of the outbreak, and is 2 SNPs from three other early Region A genomes, which is consistent with it being part of the same cluster. The genome is complete (99.4 % covered at ≥ 10x), but with only a few SNPs of difference, the resolution does not allow us to identify direct transmission links.”



Next: One-page brief template.

title: Model answer
text:
1. Are the Region C cases linked to the Region A outbreak? Probably yes. The Region C genomes belong to TV.2 and its descendants. TV.2 first appears in Region A (1–5 March, S01 on 2 March), and the first TV.2 case in Region C comes later (OB22, 12 March), only 1 SNP from OB10, an early Region A genome. The large Region C cluster (TV.2.2, 7 genomes from 25 March) descends from that same ancestor and carries 3 own mutations: it is the result of local transmission in Region C after an introduction. A TV.2.1 genome in Region C (OB14, 2 April) is 4 SNPs from a Region A TV.2.1 genome (OB23) but 10 from the local TV.2.2 cluster: a second link between the regions, not part of the local cluster. The tree cannot prove the direction of the introductions; the dates and the early appearance in Region A make “A → C” the most plausible reading.
2. Are the Region B cases part of the outbreak? No (not on these data). The Region B genomes are TV.3, 6 SNPs from the root and without any of the TV.2 mutations: an older, independent lineage. Region B and D also have TV.1 background genomes.
3. How confident, and what next? Moderate. Strengths: complete genomes, clear lineage structure, dates that agree with the tree. Limits: very few SNPs (1–3 per branch), small sample (26 genomes), no contact information, one low-quality genome excluded (OB24, 23 % N). Next steps: sequence more Region C cases and the cases between 5 and 25 March; collect travel and contact data of OB22 and OB14; re-sequence the failed samples (S02, S03).

TV.2 first appears in Region A (1–5 March, S01 on 2 March), and the first TV.2 case in Region C comes later (OB22, 12 March), only 1 SNP from OB10, an early Region A genome. The large Region C cluster (TV.2.2, 7 genomes from 25 March) descends from that same ancestor and carries 3 own mutations: it is the result of local transmission in Region C after an introduction. A TV.2.1 genome in Region C (OB14, 2 April) is 4 SNPs from a Region A TV.2.1 genome (OB23) but 10 from the local TV.2.2 cluster: a second link between the regions, not part of the local cluster. The tree cannot prove the direction of the introductions; the dates and the early appearance in Region A make “A → C” the most plausible reading.
2. Are the Region B cases part of the outbreak? No (not on these data). The Region B genomes are TV.3, 6 SNPs from the root and without any of the TV.2 mutations: an older, independent lineage. Region B and D also have TV.1 background genomes.
3. How confident, and what next? Moderate. Strengths: complete genomes, clear lineage structure, dates that agree with the tree. Limits: very few SNPs (1–3 per branch), small sample (26 genomes), no contact information, one low-quality genome excluded (OB24, 23 % N). Next steps: sequence more Region C cases and the cases between 5 and 25 March; collect travel and contact data of OB22 and OB14; re-sequence the failed samples (S02, S03).

title: Model answer
text:
Example brief (one page)

Genomic investigation brief — TOYV1, Regions A–C
Key message. The Region C cases are consistent with an introduction from Region A in early March followed by local transmission; the older Region B cases belong to a different lineage and are not part of this chain. Confidence: moderate.
Data and quality. 28 genomes received (27 outbreak + S01), 27 analysed. OB24 excluded (23 % N). Reference TOYV1. Negative control: 50 viral reads (barcode bleed); the samples concerned have > 70x and are not affected.
Findings. Lineage TV.2 first seen in Region A on 1–5 March. In Region C: one early TV.2 genome (12 March), a cluster of 7 TV.2.2 genomes (25 March–26 April) and one TV.2.1 genome (2 April). Region B: TV.3 (5 genomes) and TV.1, 16 SNPs or more from TV.2.
Figure. Tree of 27 genomes coloured by region (maximum-likelihood, 1,000 ultrafast bootstraps).
Interpretation. The pattern suggests an introduction followed by local transmission in Region C; the direction of introductions is inferred from dates, not demonstrated by the genomes.
Limits. Few SNPs (low resolution), small sample, no contact data.
Recommendations. Sequence more Region C cases and the March cases; collect travel/contact history for the early Region C and TV.2.1 cases; re-sequence samples with insufficient coverage.

title: From FASTQ to assembly: QC, trimming, assembly and identification
text:
Step 1 — Look at a read
A FASTQ file stores four lines per read: the read identifier, nucleotide sequence, a + separator, and a quality string. The files are compressed (.gz), so we use zcat.
zcat data/SRR26396743_1.fastq.gz | head -4
Questions

Which line contains the nucleotide sequence? Which contains the quality scores?
What does each character in the quality string represent?







TipAnswers






Line 1 is the read identifier, line 2 is the nucleotide sequence, line 3 is +, and line 4 contains the quality string.
Each quality character encodes the estimated confidence in the corresponding base.

title: From FASTQ to assembly: QC, trimming, assembly and identification
section: Step 2 — Quality control of the raw reads (FastQC + MultiQC)
text:
Step 2 — Quality control of the raw reads (FastQC + MultiQC)
FastQC analyzes individual FASTQ files and produces HTML reports. MultiQC combines the results into a single report.
Create an output directory:
mkdir -p results/qc_raw
Run FastQC:
fastqc -t 2 -o results/qc_raw data/SRR26396743_*.fastq.gz
Combine the reports:
multiqc results/qc_raw -o results/qc_raw
Open the report in your browser:
open results/qc_raw/multiqc_report.html
On Linux, you can use:
xdg-open results/qc_raw/multiqc_report.html
Examine three sections:

General Statistics: number of reads, sequence length, and overall quality indicators.
Per base sequence quality: quality distribution along the reads.
Adapter Content: evidence of adapter sequences remaining in the reads.

title: From FASTQ to assembly: QC, trimming, assembly and identification
text:
Step 3 — Trim reads with fastp
fastp can detect adapters in paired-end data, trim low-quality tails, filter short reads, and generate quality-control reports.
Create the output directories:
mkdir -p results/trimmed results/trimmomatic
Run trimmomatic:
trimmomatic PE \
  -threads 2 \
  -phred33 \
  data/SRR26396743_1.fastq \
  data/SRR26396743_2.fastq \
  results/trimmed/SRR26396743_1_paired.fastq.gz \
  results/trimmed/SRR26396743_1_unpaired.fastq.gz \
  results/trimmed/SRR26396743_2_paired.fastq.gz \
  results/trimmed/SRR26396743_2_unpaired.fastq.gz \
  TRAILING:20 \
  SLIDINGWINDOW:4:20 \
  MINLEN:50
What do the options mean?

PE: Processes paired-end reads.
-threads 2: Uses two CPU threads.
-phred33: Specifies the Phred+33 quality score encoding.
TRAILING:20: Removes low-quality bases from the ends of reads when their quality score is below 20.
SLIDINGWINDOW:4:20: Trims a read when the average quality score in a four-base sliding window falls below 20.
MINLEN:50: Discards reads shorter than 50 bases after trimming.
paired: Output files containing reads whose mates both pass filtering.
unpaired: Output files containing reads whose mates do not both pass filtering.

section: Step 6 — Which organisms are in the reads? (Kraken2 or BLAST)
text:
Step 6 — Which organisms are in the reads? (Kraken2 or BLAST)
Assembling is not enough: we must verify that the sequences really come from the expected organism, and detect possible contamination (human DNA, bacteria, other viruses). Two complementary approaches are available.

Option A — Kraken2 on the reads
Kraken2 assigns a taxonomic label to each read by comparing its k-mers to a reference database. It is fast and gives an overview of all the organisms in the sample.
Create the output directory:
mkdir -p results/kraken2
Run Kraken2 on the trimmed read pairs. Replace db/kraken2 with the path of the Kraken2 database provided for the course:
kraken2 \
  --db db/kraken2 \
  --paired \
  --gzip-compressed \
  --threads 2 \
  --report results/kraken2/SRR26396743.report \
  --output results/kraken2/SRR26396743.kraken \
  results/trimmed/SRR26396743_1.fastq.gz \
  results/trimmed/SRR26396743_2.fastq.gz
Look at the taxonomic summary:
head -20 results/kraken2/SRR26396743.report
The report has six columns: percentage of reads in the clade, number of reads in the clade, number of reads assigned directly to the taxon, rank code (U unclassified, D domain, G genus, S species, …), NCBI taxonomy ID, and scientific name.
Show only the species-level lines, sorted by percentage:
awk '$4=="S"' results/kraken2/SRR26396743.report | sort -k1,1nr | head -10
Note: a complete Kraken2 database (e.g. Standard) is very large. For this practical, a small database (such as a viral or MiniKraken index) is sufficient. Indexes are listed at https://benlangmead.github.io/aws-indexes/k2.


Option B — BLAST on the contigs
BLAST aligns a sequence against a reference database and reports the best matches. It is slower but more precise, and works well on a few long contigs.
Extract the longest contig:
seqkit sort -l -r results/spades/contigs.fasta | seqkit head -n 1 > results/spades/longest_contig.fasta
Run blastn against the NCBI nucleotide database (remote search, internet connection required):
blastn \
  -query results/spades/longest_contig.fasta \
  -db nt \
  -remote \
  -max_target_seqs 5 \
  -outfmt "6 qseqid sseqid stitle pident length evalue bitscore" \
  -out results/spades/longest_contig.blast.tsv
cat results/spades/longest_contig.blast.tsv
The columns are: query ID, subject ID, subject title, percent identity, alignment length, E-value, and bit score.
You can also paste the sequence into the web interface: https://blast.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/Blast.cgi (choose Nucleotide BLAST).

title: Coverage and consensus
text:
Goal: Measure genome coverage, identify low-depth regions, build a consensus genome, and identify candidate variants.
We will analyze the SARS-CoV-2 sequencing run SRR26396743 from NCBI, using the trimmed reads and BAM file generated in the previous sessions.
Input files
If a previous step failed, use the corresponding precomputed files provided with the course, if available.

title: Coverage and consensus
section: Step 1 — Calculate depth at every position
text:
Step 1 — Calculate depth at every position
Depth is the number of reads covering a reference position. We use -a to include positions with zero coverage.
Create the output directories:
mkdir -p results/coverage results/consensus results/variants
Calculate the depth:
samtools depth -aa \
  results/bam/SRR26396743.bam \
  > results/coverage/SRR26396743.depth.tsv
Inspect the first three lines:
head -3 results/coverage/SRR26396743.depth.tsv
The output contains three columns:

Reference sequence name
Position
Read depth

Obtain a summary with Samtools:
samtools coverage results/bam/SRR26396743.bam
Questions

What is the depth at the first three reference positions?
Are there positions with zero coverage?
What are the mean depth and percentage of the reference covered by at least one read?

Answer
The depth varies along the genome. A position with zero coverage has no aligned reads supporting a base call. The summary values must be obtained from your own output.

title: Coverage and consensus
section: Step 2 — Calculate mean depth and genome breadth at ≥10×
text:
Step 2 — Calculate mean depth and genome breadth at ≥10×
For this exercise, we will use 10× depth as a practical threshold for assessing genome completeness.

Mean depth: average number of reads covering each reference position.
Breadth at ≥10×: percentage of reference positions covered by at least 10 reads.

Run:
awk '{
  total += $3
  if ($3 >= 10) covered++
  positions++
}
END {
  if (positions > 0) {
    printf "Mean depth: %.1f\n", total/positions
    printf "Genome at >=10x: %.1f%%\n", 100*covered/positions
  }
}' results/coverage/SRR26396743.depth.tsv
Questions

What is the mean depth?
What percentage of the genome has at least 10× coverage?
Does the mean depth alone tell you whether the genome is complete?

Answer
No. A high mean depth can coexist with poorly covered regions. Always examine both mean depth and breadth of coverage.

title: Coverage and consensus
Coverage and consensus
text:
Step 4 — Visualize coverage in IGV
Open IGV and load:

Reference: data/ncbi/SARS-CoV-2_NC_045512.2.fasta
Alignment: results/bam/SRR26396743.bam

Inspect one of the low-depth intervals identified in Step 3.
Questions

Is coverage uniform across the region?
Is the region completely uncovered or only poorly covered?
Do reads stop abruptly at a particular coordinate?
What additional information would help determine why the region has low coverage?

Answer
IGV helps distinguish a complete coverage gap from a region with reduced depth. The shape of the coverage profile may suggest a technical issue, but further information about the library preparation and sequencing protocol is needed to establish the cause.

title: Coverage and consensus
section: Step 5 — Build the consensus genome with iVar
text:
Step 5 — Build the consensus genome with iVar
A consensus genome represents the most strongly supported nucleotide at each reference position, subject to the calling thresholds.
Here, we will use:

Minimum base quality: Q20
Minimum depth: 10 reads
Minimum proportion of reads supporting a base: 50%
Missing or insufficiently supported positions: N

Run samtools mpileup and pass its output to ivar consensus:
samtools mpileup \
  -aa -A -d 0 -Q 0 \
  -f data/ncbi/SARS-CoV-2_NC_045512.2.fasta \
  results/bam/SRR26396743.bam \
  | ivar consensus \
      -p results/consensus/SRR26396743 \
      -q 20 \
      -t 0.5 \
      -m 10 \
      -n N
This produces a consensus FASTA file, normally named:
results/consensus/SRR26396743.fa
Inspect its header and sequence:
head -c 300 results/consensus/SRR26396743.fa
Questions

What is the length of the consensus?
Why are some positions represented by N?
What happens when a position has fewer than 10 reads?
Does a consensus sequence necessarily represent a perfect reconstruction of the original viral genome?

Answer
A consensus can contain N where the evidence is insufficient under the selected thresholds. It is an estimate derived from the available reads, not a guarantee of a perfectly reconstructed genome.
The consensus quality depends on depth, base quality, mapping quality, the consensus thresholds, and the quality of the underlying sequencing data.

title: Coverage and consensus
section: Step 6 — Measure the number of ambiguous bases
text:
Step 6 — Measure the number of ambiguous bases
Count the number of N bases:
grep -v '^>' results/consensus/SRR26396743.fa \
  | tr -cd 'N' \
  | wc -c
Calculate the percentage of the consensus represented by N:
awk '
  /^>/ {next}
  {
    n += gsub(/N/, "&")
    length_total += length($0)
  }
  END {
    if (length_total > 0)
      printf "N bases: %d\nN percentage: %.2f%%\n",
             n, 100*n/length_total
  }
' results/consensus/SRR26396743.fa
Find the longest consecutive run of N bases:
grep -v '^>' results/consensus/SRR26396743.fa \
  | tr -d '\n' \
  | grep -o 'N\+' \
  | awk '{print length}' \
  | sort -n \
  | tail -1
If no N bases are present, the last command produces no output; interpret that as zero.
Questions

How many N bases are present?
What percentage of the consensus is ambiguous?
What is the longest consecutive run of N?
Where are the longest ambiguous regions located?

Answer
All values should be measured from the generated consensus. A large number of N bases or a long consecutive run indicates regions that cannot be confidently resolved with the chosen thresholds.

title: Coverage and consensus
section: Step 7 — Identify candidate variants with bcftools
text:
Step 7 — Identify candidate variants with bcftools
We will compare the aligned reads with the reference to identify candidate single-nucleotide variants and short insertions or deletions.
Generate a VCF file:
bcftools mpileup \
  -f data/ncbi/SARS-CoV-2_NC_045512.2.fasta \
  -Q 20 \
  -d 1000000 \
  -a AD \
  results/bam/SRR26396743.bam \
  | bcftools call \
      -mv \
      --ploidy 1 \
      -Oz \
      -o results/variants/SRR26396743.vcf.gz
Index the VCF:
bcftools index results/variants/SRR26396743.vcf.gz
Display the variant records:
bcftools view -H results/variants/SRR26396743.vcf.gz \
  | cut -f1,2,4,5,6
The columns displayed are:

Reference sequence
Position
Reference allele
Alternative allele
Variant quality (QUAL)

Count the reported variant records:
bcftools view -H results/variants/SRR26396743.vcf.gz \
  | wc -l
Questions

How many variant records were reported?
Which reference positions contain candidate variants?
Do the variants have good read support?
Can you confirm that a variant is real based only on its presence in the VCF?

Answer
The VCF contains candidate variants identified by the caller. Each candidate must be interpreted using its read depth, allele support, base quality, mapping quality, and alignment context.
A variant record is not automatically proof of a biological mutation. Examine suspicious calls in IGV and apply suitable quality filters before downstream analyses.

title: Coverage and consensus
section: Step 8 — Change the consensus depth threshold
text:
Step 8 — Change the consensus depth threshold
A higher minimum depth can make the consensus more conservative, but it can also increase the number of ambiguous bases.
Build a second consensus requiring at least 30 reads per position:
samtools mpileup \
  -aa -A -d 0 -Q 0 \
  -f data/ncbi/SARS-CoV-2_NC_045512.2.fasta \
  results/bam/SRR26396743.bam \
  | ivar consensus \
      -p results/consensus/SRR26396743.m30 \
      -q 20 \
      -t 0.5 \
      -m 30 \
      -n N
Count the ambiguous bases in the second consensus:
grep -v '^>' results/consensus/SRR26396743.m30.fa \
  | tr -cd 'N' \
  | wc -c
Compare the results with the consensus generated at 10×.
Questions

Did the number of N bases change?
Did the consensus become more or less complete?
Why might a laboratory choose a higher depth threshold?

Answer
A higher threshold may increase the number of ambiguous bases because positions supported by 10–29 reads no longer meet the minimum-depth requirement. This illustrates the trade-off between the completeness of the consensus and the strictness of the calling criteria.
A suitable threshold depends on the sequencing protocol, the intended use, and the laboratory’s validated quality criteria.

title: Coverage and consensus
text:
Final question
The genome has a mean depth of 100×, but 15% of its positions have zero coverage. Can you consider the consensus complete?
Answer
No. Mean depth is an average and can conceal large coverage gaps. Assess mean depth, breadth at relevant thresholds, low-depth intervals, and the number and distribution of N bases before deciding whether a consensus is suitable for its intended purpose.
Next: Is this genome good enough?
